metric_rationale: This is a per-trial dissociation score exploiting both orthogonal dissociations in the design, rewritten as flat, dependency-free code (no imports, no nested functions, no try/except, no lambdas) to eliminate the transmission-level syntax failures of the previous two attempts. Construction: on each trial I compute (i) the TTB pick — the features are listed in descending-validity order (validities [0.95, 0.85, 0.75, 0.65, 0.5]), so the TTB cascade is just the lowest-index feature on which the two options differ — and (ii) the Tallying pick from strict feature-wise win counts. Trials where both theories agree (types 11-12, 16 trials/subject) are skipped. On full dissociation trials (types 1-6, 48 trials/subject), where TTB backs the option with FEWER cue wins and Tallying backs the majority-tally option, a choice matching TTB contributes +1 and one matching Tallying contributes -1. On tied-tally trials (types 7-10, 32 trials/subject), Tallying is structurally forced to exactly p=0.5 for every parameter value (softmax over tied scores is uniform and the lapse injects uniform), so any systematic choice is pure TTB signal: +0.5 toward TTB's pick, -0.5 away. Expected value under TTB-simulated data is 0.8*(2q-1) with q=(1-eps)*sigmoid(beta)+eps/2, which is strictly positive for any beta>0, eps<0.5; under Tallying-simulated data it is -0.6*avg(2p_margin-1), strictly negative for any beta>0. The mean gap is order 0.3-1.0 across plausible parameters while per-subject sd is only ~0.05-0.10 (80 informative trials pooled), giving a decisive Welch's t-test at N=25. The score is self-hedging: if TTB is simulated with weak beta, the tied-trial component still adds signal while dissociation trials shrink, and vice versa for weak Tallying parameters. The function is a simple mean of per-trial contributions, so it works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices, making the between-subject variance well defined.

The design factorially crosses the tally margin d (the ONLY input Tallying's prediction depends on) with the top-cue direction s (the ONLY input TTB's prediction depends on). I exploit both main effects simultaneously with a single OLS coefficient contrast: regress the chose-A indicator on [intercept, d, s] over all trials and return b_d - b_s. Under Tallying, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*d) + eps/2, so the partial slope on d is strictly positive (up to ~0.125 per unit d when beta is large) while the partial slope on s is exactly 0 — s adds nothing once d is controlled. Under TTB, p(A) = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*s) + eps/2, so the partial slope on s is strictly positive (up to 0.5) while the partial slope on d is exactly 0 — within a fixed s-column TTB is flat in d by construction, and no (beta, eps) can change that. Hence the metric is positive under Tallying and negative under TTB, with a gap equal to the SUM of the two theories' signature effect sizes, making it robust: it discriminates even if one theory happens to be simulated with weak parameters, as long as the other shows its signature. Including s as a regressor also removes the mild d-s collinearity built into the 16 pairs (corr ~ 0.3), so the d-coefficient is a clean within-column slope rather than a confounded marginal. Per-subject computation is well-conditioned: every subject sees all 16 pair types x 6 reps (96 trials), d spans -4..+4 within each s-column, and the regressors are balanced (mean d = 0, eight s=+1 and eight s=-1 types). Per-subject sampling noise of b_d is small (~0.02) because it borrows strength across all nine d levels, and noise on b_s (~0.11 worst case, p=0.5) is dwarfed by TTB's s-effect (~0.5 at moderate beta). At N=25 the Welch t-test on the pooled point estimates with these between-subject variances yields a highly significant separation in every non-degenerate parameter regime.
